strongest_form: Lions, wolves and orcas eat other animals without anyone calling it evil, and humans descend from a long line of animals that hunted and scavenged. If killing animals for food were wrong in itself, it would be wrong everywhere in nature, yet nobody thinks a lion is doing something immoral. Eating meat is part of what we are.
text: Lions eat meat, wolves eat meat, and our ancestors hunted for a very long time. Why would it suddenly be wrong when we do it?
key_points: Separate what animals do from what moral agents ought to do: lions cannot reflect on alternatives or survive without meat
Address that humans can choose among diets and, in most places, can do well without animal products
Concede that eating meat is natural without letting 'natural' settle whether it is right
Point out that having the power to do something does not make it right, since the same reasoning would excuse harming vulnerable people; the question is whether the harm is justified
sources: Singer, P. (1975). Animal Liberation. New York: New York Review, distributed by Random House.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Humans have canine teeth, a digestive system that handles meat well, and a long record of eating it. The usual comparison with gorillas or cows is selective: our anatomy looks like that of a flexible omnivore, which suggests meat is a normal part of a human diet and not an addition to it.
text: We've got canine teeth and we digest meat perfectly well. Doesn't our anatomy say we're omnivores?
key_points: Concede that humans are physiologically capable omnivores
Explain that being able to digest meat does not make it necessary or morally permissible
Avoid leaning on the claim that human canines are small so we are herbivores, because teeth alone are weak evidence either way
sources: Ungar, P. S. (2012). Dental evidence for the reconstruction of diet in African early Homo. Current Anthropology 53(S6): S318-S329.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Archaeological evidence for butchery goes back a very long way, and one influential hypothesis holds that animal foods and later cooking allowed the human gut to shrink while the brain grew. Even if we can live well on plants today, a diet that excludes animal foods cuts against the biology that made us the species we are.
text: Eating meat and cooking food is a big part of why we evolved large brains. Isn't cutting out animal foods going against what made us human?
key_points: Accept that animal foods and cooking plausibly played a role in human evolution, while noting how debated the size of that role is
Separate evolutionary origins from present nutritional need: what helped then is not required now, given modern food, fortification and supplements
Avoid claiming that early humans were vegan or that the evidence settles the question the other way
sources: Aiello, L. C. & Wheeler, P. (1995). The expensive-tissue hypothesis. Current Anthropology 36(2): 199-221.
Milton, K. (1999). A hypothesis to explain the role of meat-eating in human evolution. Evolutionary Anthropology 8(1): 11-21.

strongest_form: Cats are obligate carnivores and need nutrients, such as taurine, that occur naturally in animal tissue. If a vegan keeps a cat, they are buying animal products in bulk, and if they refuse to keep carnivorous pets, they are leaving animals without homes. Either way the position seems to conflict with caring about animals.
text: I feed my cat meat because cats are obligate carnivores. If animal products are wrong, isn't keeping carnivorous pets just as bad?
key_points: Concede that cats have real nutritional needs and that vets, not online advice, should guide any change to a pet's diet
Distinguish a duty to animals you have taken responsibility for from a discretionary human choice: humans are not obligate carnivores
Avoid pretending the tension is trivial, since many vegans disagree about how to handle it
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: If animal suffering matters in itself, nature is full of it: predation, parasites, starvation and disease. Vegans do not try to stop lions, which suggests the concern is selective and about discomfort with human action, not about suffering as such. A principle that only applies when humans are involved is a different principle.
text: If you care so much about animal suffering, why aren't you trying to stop lions killing gazelles? Your ethics only seem to kick in when humans are involved.
key_points: Distinguish duties not to harm from duties to rescue, and responsibility for one's own actions
Acknowledge that concern for wild animal suffering is a real philosophical position, and that practical limits on intervening are serious
Avoid romanticising nature or claiming that wild animals do not suffer
sources: Horta, O. (2010). Debunking the idyllic view of natural processes: population dynamics and suffering in the wild. Telos 17: 73-88.

strongest_form: Our closest relatives are not strict herbivores. Chimpanzees hunt monkeys and eat insects, and most primates take some animal food when they can. The best reading of the evidence is that humans are opportunistic omnivores, and a fully plant-based diet is the outlier among primates.
text: Chimps hunt and eat meat, and so do plenty of other primates. Isn't the natural primate diet mixed, not plant-only?
key_points: Accept that chimpanzees and many primates eat some animal foods
Explain why primate behaviour is weak guidance for what humans ought to eat or do
Note that primate diets are mostly plant-based, without pretending that occasional meat-eating is irrelevant
sources: Stanford, C. B. (1996). The hunting ecology of wild chimpanzees: implications for the evolutionary ecology of Pliocene hominids. American Anthropologist 98(1): 96-113.

strongest_form: In many regions, predators have been removed and deer or other wild populations grow until they destroy woodland and starve. Culling is often the responsible management response. If culling is justified, eating the meat is better than wasting it, and hunters do real ecological work that vegans cannot replace.
text: In a lot of places deer have to be culled because their predators are gone. If that's necessary, isn't eating the meat the responsible thing to do?
key_points: Concede that culling can be ecologically justified in some places
Distinguish eating culled wildlife from supplying a general diet with farmed meat, which is not possible at that scale
Address that predator removal and human land use created the problem in the first place
sources: Cote, S. D., Rooney, T. P., Tremblay, J.-P., Dussault, C. & Waller, D. M. (2004). Ecological impacts of deer overabundance. Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 35: 113-147.

strongest_form: Cattle, sheep and chickens are the product of thousands of years of co-evolution with humans. As species they exist in vast numbers because people eat them, and a world without animal farming would see most of these breeds disappear. A relationship that benefits both sides at the species level is hard to call simple exploitation, and abolishing it is not obviously a kindness to the animals.
text: Cows, sheep and chickens exist in huge numbers because humans eat them. Isn't that more like a partnership between species than exploitation?
key_points: Distinguish species-level success from individual welfare, since interests belong to individual animals and not to breeds
Address that selective breeding has caused serious welfare problems in many farmed breeds

Point out that the 'partnership' framing assumes both sides chose it: farmed animals cannot consent to or leave the arrangement. Whether they would exist otherwise is a separate question (the larder argument)
sources: Diamond, J. (2002). Evolution, consequences and future of plant and animal domestication. Nature 418: 700-707.

strongest_form: Animal protein contains all the essential amino acids in proportions close to what people need, and it is generally more digestible. Most plant proteins are lower in at least one essential amino acid and are digested less completely. Vegans can meet their needs, but only by planning in a way omnivores never have to.
text: Plant protein is incomplete and less digestible than animal protein. Can you really get the same quality without meat?
key_points: Accept that plant proteins differ from animal proteins in amino acid profile and digestibility on average
Explain that a varied mix of plant foods can meet requirements, and that complementary proteins do not need to be matched meal by meal
Avoid claiming that plant protein is identical to animal protein on every measure
sources: Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.
FAO (2013). Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition. FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 92.
Mariotti, F. & Gardner, C. D. (2019). Dietary protein and amino acids in vegetarian diets - a review. Nutrients 11(11): 2661.
van Vliet, S., Burd, N. A. & van Loon, L. J. C. (2015). The skeletal muscle anabolic response to plant- versus animal-based protein consumption. Journal of Nutrition 145(9): 1981-1991.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Vitamin B12 cannot be reliably obtained from unfortified plant foods, and deficiency can cause serious and sometimes irreversible harm. A diet that has to be topped up with a supplement or fortified food to avoid illness is not a complete diet. If it were truly suited to humans, it would not depend on technology to be safe.
text: Vegans have to take B12 supplements or they get ill. Doesn't that prove it isn't a complete diet?
key_points: Acknowledge that supplements or fortified foods are genuinely required, not optional
Note that B12 is made by microorganisms and that livestock are themselves often given B12 through feed or supplements
Address that needing a supplement is not the same as being unhealthy, since many diets rely on fortification
sources: Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.
EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (2015). Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for cobalamin (vitamin B12). EFSA Journal 13(7): 4150.

Gilsing, A. M. J. et al. (2010). Serum concentrations of vitamin B12 and folate in British male omnivores, vegetarians and vegans: results from the EPIC-Oxford cohort study. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition 64: 933-939.
NHS. The vegan diet (nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/the-vegan-diet/).
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Children are growing quickly and have less margin for error with energy, B12, iron, zinc, iodine and long-chain fatty acids. Professional bodies differ: some say well-planned vegan diets can be adequate at every life stage, while others will not recommend them for children on the current evidence. 'Well-planned' is doing a lot of work, and the person making the choice is the parent, not the child. Even a small rate of deficiency in this group can have lasting effects, so why accept the risk for someone who cannot consent?
text: Children grow fast and can't consent. Even if vegan adults can manage, isn't it irresponsible to put a child on a diet where one planning mistake could cause lasting harm?
key_points: State that well-planned vegan diets need B12 from supplements or fortified foods, and that families should consult a registered dietitian or doctor
Acknowledge the higher stakes during growth and development, and that the evidence base for children is thinner than for adults
Address the consent point: parents shape children's diets in every household, so compare risks with a poorly planned omnivore diet, without dismissing the risk
Note that position statements differ between bodies and have changed over time, so say which one you are relying on and avoid presenting the question as settled either way
sources: Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.
Sutter, D. O. & Bender, N. (2021). Nutrient status and growth in vegan children. Nutrition Research 91: 13-25.
Klug, A. et al. (2024). Update of the DGE position on vegan diet: position statement of the German Nutrition Society (DGE). Ernaehrungs Umschau 71(7): 60-84.
Richter, M. et al. (2016). Vegan diet: position of the German Nutrition Society (DGE). Ernaehrungs Umschau 63(4): 92-102 (earlier position, superseded by the 2024 update).

strongest_form: Iron and zinc in plant foods are absorbed less well, partly because phytates and other compounds bind them, and haem iron from meat is taken up more efficiently than non-haem iron. Vegans may therefore have lower iron stores and need to pay deliberate attention to food choices and preparation to keep up.
text: Iron and zinc from plants are absorbed much less efficiently than from meat. Doesn't that put vegans at a real disadvantage?
key_points: Accept that non-haem iron and zinc are less bioavailable on average
Explain that absorption adjusts when stores are low and can be improved through food choices and preparation
Note that iron deficiency also occurs in omnivores, while some vegan groups do show higher risk
sources: Hunt, J. R. (2003). Bioavailability of iron, zinc, and other trace minerals from vegetarian diets. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 78(3 Suppl): 633S-639S.
Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Plants supply the short-chain omega-3 ALA, but humans convert only a limited amount to the long-chain forms EPA and DHA, which matter for the brain and the heart. Oily fish is the main dietary source, so vegans rely on algae-based supplements to fill a gap that omnivores fill with food.
text: The omega-3s that matter, EPA and DHA, mostly come from fish. Plant sources convert poorly, so don't vegans need yet another supplement?
key_points: Acknowledge that conversion of ALA to EPA and DHA is limited and varies between people
Note that algae provide EPA and DHA directly, and that fish accumulate them from algae
Avoid claiming that flaxseed or similar foods fully replace long-chain omega-3, and avoid treating the evidence for benefit as settled in every respect

Mention that fish also carry mercury and other pollutants, and that NHS advice limits oily fish to two portions a week in pregnancy and says to avoid shark, swordfish and marlin; use this as a caution only, not as an argument against eating fish
sources: Burdge, G. C. & Calder, P. C. (2005). Conversion of alpha-linolenic acid to longer-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in human adults. Reproduction Nutrition Development 45(5): 581-597.
NHS. Fish and shellfish nutrition (NHS website, Live Well: Eat well).
Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.

strongest_form: Soy contains isoflavones, which act like weak oestrogens, and vegan diets often rely on soy heavily. Some people worry about hormonal effects, thyroid function and fertility. Building a diet that already needs careful planning on a food with those questions attached is a risk that meat-eaters do not take.
text: Vegans live on soy, and soy is full of oestrogen-like compounds. Isn't that a hormone problem waiting to happen?
key_points: Explain that isoflavones are plant compounds that are not equivalent to human oestrogen, and that clinical evidence in adults has generally not shown feminising effects
Acknowledge that research is not fully settled for every outcome and group, and that people with thyroid conditions should take medical advice
Note that a vegan diet does not have to depend on soy
sources: Messina, M. (2016). Soy and health update: evaluation of the clinical and epidemiologic literature. Nutrients 8(12): 754.
Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: A large online survey of US adults found that most of the people who had tried a vegetarian or vegan diet no longer followed it. That attrition may signal that these diets are hard to sustain or leave some people feeling unwell, and individual accounts of fatigue and deficiency are too common to dismiss as people simply doing it wrong.
text: Loads of people try veganism and quit because they feel awful. If it were a healthy default, would so many go back?
key_points: Acknowledge that high lapse rates are documented, while noting the figure is a one-off snapshot of self-reported history and that about a third of lapsers had followed the diet for three months or less

Separate the reasons people stop (social difficulty, convenience, cravings, poor planning, deficiency) from whether a well-planned diet is adequate; in that survey most lapsers reported none of the listed health problems
Avoid dismissing individual experience as simply 'not doing it properly'
Say plainly that B12 from a supplement or fortified food is essential, and that persistent fatigue is something to raise with a GP or dietitian, not to self-diagnose
sources: Asher, K. et al. (2014). Study of Current and Former Vegetarians and Vegans: Initial Findings. Faunalytics (formerly Humane Research Council), with companion tables and methodology (faunalytics.org/study-of-current-and-former-vegetarians-and-vegans/).
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Claims that vegans are healthier rest largely on observational studies, and people who choose veganism tend to smoke less, drink less and exercise more. Statistical adjustment cannot remove all of that healthy-user bias, and some cohorts even show signals such as higher fracture or stroke risk. The evidence supports 'a diet rich in whole plant foods is good for you' much better than 'excluding animal foods is good for you'.
text: The studies showing vegans are healthier are mostly observational and full of healthy-user bias. How do you know it's the lack of meat, not everything else vegans do?
key_points: Accept that most of the evidence is observational and vulnerable to confounding
Distinguish a diet rich in whole plant foods from simply excluding animal products, noting that vegan junk food exists
Acknowledge the mixed findings (for example lower heart disease risk in some cohorts, higher fracture risk in some) without overclaiming either way
sources: Appleby, P. N. & Key, T. J. (2016). The long-term health of vegetarians and vegans. Proceedings of the Nutrition Society 75(3): 287-293.

Tong, T. Y. N. et al. (2019). Risks of ischaemic heart disease and stroke in meat eaters, fish eaters, and vegetarians over 18 years of follow-up: results from the prospective EPIC-Oxford study. BMJ 366: l4897.
Tong, T. Y. N. et al. (2020). Vegetarian and vegan diets and risks of total and site-specific fractures: results from the prospective EPIC-Oxford study. BMC Medicine 18: 353.
Bakaloudi, D. R. et al. (2021). Intake and adequacy of the vegan diet. A systematic review of the evidence. Clinical Nutrition 40(5): 3503-3521.

strongest_form: Athletes have high protein and energy needs. Plant proteins are on average less digestible and lower in some amino acids, so a vegan athlete has to plan more carefully, and elite performance is where small nutritional shortfalls show first.
text: Elite performance needs a lot of protein and quick recovery. Can a vegan really build muscle and compete at a high level, or are those athletes the exception?
key_points: Acknowledge that athletes need more energy and protein and that planning matters more for them; the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics position says well-planned vegan diets can suit athletes

Note that one 12-week trial in young men found similar muscle gains on protein-matched vegan and omnivorous diets, and a study of recreational runners found similar exercise capacity, while stressing that these studies are small and short and neither involved elite athletes
Avoid claiming a vegan diet improves performance; the evidence points to comparable performance, not an advantage
Mention that B12 needs a supplement and that a registered dietitian or sports nutritionist can check iron, vitamin D and total energy, and do not give individual advice
sources: Hevia-Larraín, V. et al. (2021). High-protein plant-based diet versus a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations: a comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores. Sports Medicine 51(6): 1317-1330.
Nebl, J. et al. (2019). Exercise capacity of vegan, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and omnivorous recreational runners. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition 16: 23.
Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.

strongest_form: Studies of vegans show lower average iodine intake, vitamin D status falls in winter, and calcium can fall short without fortified foods. A diet that only works with fortification, supplements and planning is more fragile than one that meets these needs from ordinary food.
text: Beyond B12, vegans are at risk of low iodine, vitamin D and calcium. Isn't a diet that needs several supplements and careful tracking a poor fit for most people?
key_points: Acknowledge that iodine is a real concern: most plant drinks are not iodine-fortified and vegans have lower iodine status on average, so it needs deliberate planning, and seaweed is an unreliable fix because its iodine content varies widely and can be excessive
Note that UK guidance advises everyone to consider vitamin D in autumn and winter, so this is not a problem unique to vegans
Cover calcium through fortified drinks, calcium-set tofu and some greens, and acknowledge that vegans had a higher fracture risk in a large UK cohort, which the authors linked to lower calcium intake
Say B12 is not optional and send the person to a GP or registered dietitian for personal advice and blood tests, without giving individual doses
sources: Eveleigh, E. R. et al. (2020). Vegans, vegetarians, and omnivores: how does dietary choice influence iodine intake? A systematic review. Nutrients 12(6): 1606.
Bath, S. C. et al. (2017). Iodine concentration of milk-alternative drinks available in the UK in comparison with cows' milk. British Journal of Nutrition 118(7): 525-532.
Appleby, P. et al. (2007). Comparative fracture risk in vegetarians and nonvegetarians in EPIC-Oxford. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition 61(12): 1400-1406.
Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition (2016). Vitamin D and Health. Public Health England.

strongest_form: The strongest cancer evidence concerns processed meat. Fresh red meat is classed as probably carcinogenic on more limited evidence, and for moderate intake the absolute increase in risk is small. Avoiding it entirely on cancer grounds overstates what the evidence supports.
text: The cancer warnings are about bacon and sausages, not plain fresh meat, and almost everything seems to get blamed for cancer these days. Isn't unprocessed red meat fine?
key_points: Concede the distinction: IARC classes processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and unprocessed red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) on limited evidence
Explain that these classes describe how strong the evidence is, not how large the risk is, so processed meat is not as dangerous as tobacco even though both are in Group 1

Frame risk as relative and absolute: IARC estimated about 18 percent higher bowel cancer risk per 50 g of processed meat eaten daily, which it describes as a small increase, so the absolute change for one person is small
Avoid saying all meat causes cancer, since IARC says red meat has not been established as a cause; refer personal questions to a GP or dietitian, and note that a vegan diet needs B12 supplementation
sources: Bouvard, V. et al. (2015). Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat. The Lancet Oncology 16(16): 1599-1600. (summarises the IARC Monographs Volume 114 evaluation)
IARC (2015). Q&A on the carcinogenicity of the consumption of red meat and processed meat. IARC Monographs Volume 114.

strongest_form: Harvesting crops kills field mice, rabbits, snakes and ground-nesting birds, and pesticides and machinery kill many more small animals. A vegan diet is therefore not free of animal deaths, and the claim to be avoiding killing is overstated.
text: Harvesting crops kills mice, rabbits and loads of other small animals. Doesn't that mean vegans have blood on their hands too?
key_points: Concede that crop production causes animal deaths
Address that a large share of cropland grows feed for livestock, so animal agriculture generally needs more cropland per unit of food than eating plants directly
Distinguish foreseen but unintended harm from deliberate killing, and note that the aim is reducing harm, not achieving purity
sources: Fischer, B. & Lamey, A. (2018). Field deaths in plant agriculture. Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 31: 409-428.
Our World in Data. Land use of diets (ourworldindata.org/land-use-diets).
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Plants respond to damage, release chemical alarm signals and communicate with each other through the soil. If the argument rests on avoiding suffering, we cannot be certain plants do not experience something, so the vegan line is drawn at a point that feels intuitive but is not clearly principled.
text: Plants react to being damaged and even send out warning signals. How can you be so sure they don't feel pain?
key_points: Distinguish responsiveness to stimuli from subjective experience, noting that plants have no nervous system or brain
Acknowledge residual uncertainty about plant sentience while explaining why it is far weaker than the evidence for animals
Note that even if plants did feel, eating plants directly would harm fewer of them than feeding them to animals first
sources: Taiz, L. et al. (2019). Plants neither possess nor require consciousness. Trends in Plant Science 24(8): 677-687.
Mallatt, J., Blatt, M. R., Draguhn, A., Robinson, D. G. & Taiz, L. (2021). Debunking a myth: plant consciousness. Protoplasma 258: 459-476.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: There is a real difference between a factory farm and a small pasture-based farm where animals live well and are killed quickly. Opposing the worst abuses is sensible, but treating a well-kept animal killed painlessly as morally equal to factory farming overstates the case. A good life ended humanely can be defended as better for the animal than the alternatives.
text: I only buy high-welfare meat from a local farm where the animals have a good life. Surely that's ethically different from factory farming?
key_points: Acknowledge that welfare differs enormously between systems and that high-welfare farming is better than intensive farming
Address whether killing an animal that would otherwise go on living is itself a harm, even if the death is painless
Address practical limits: how much high-welfare supply exists, whether labels match reality, and welfare issues in breeding, transport and slaughter

Ask what 'humane' covers when a healthy animal is killed at a small fraction of its natural lifespan (broiler chickens at about six weeks and pigs at about six months, against natural lifespans of years)
sources: Fraser, D. (2008). Understanding Animal Welfare: The Science in its Cultural Context. Wiley-Blackwell.
Mellor, D. J. (2016). Moving beyond the 'Five Freedoms' by updating the 'Five Provisions' and introducing aligned 'Animal Welfare Aims'. Animals 6(10): 59.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: If the reason to avoid animal products is sentience, bivalves such as mussels and oysters are a hard case: they have no brain and only a simple nervous system, and the evidence that they can suffer is thin. By a harm-based ethic they look acceptable, and where vegans refuse them anyway it suggests that veganism works as an identity rule, not as a principle about harm.
text: Oysters and mussels have no brain. If vegans care about suffering, why isn't eating them fine?
key_points: Acknowledge that bivalves are plausibly consistent with a harm-based ethic and that some vegans accept them
Say plainly that direct evidence on bivalve sentience is very limited, and that the stronger evidence for cephalopods and decapods shows the line is drawn by evidence, not by taxonomy
Explain the difference between a principle and the simple bright-line rule most vegans adopt
Keep the environmental case for bivalve farming separate from the sentience question
sources: Schotanus, J., van de Vis, H. & Steins, N. (2022). Welfare of bivalves in aquaculture? A first literature scan and plan for a comprehensive search. Wageningen Marine Research report C057/22 (doi.org/10.18174/577988).

Birch, J., Burn, C., Schnell, A., Browning, H. & Crump, A. (2021). Review of the evidence of sentience in cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans. London School of Economics and Political Science (cited for the cephalopod and decapod contrast only; it does not cover bivalves).

strongest_form: There is credible evidence that at least some insects can feel something like pain. If so, pesticides, harvesting and habitat conversion kill vast numbers of insects in any large-scale crop system, and vegans cannot claim the high ground on sentience while accepting that. If insects are not sentient, farming them for protein is a sustainable option that the vegan position does not clearly rule out. Either way the line looks hard to defend.
text: Insects might be sentient, and farming kills them in enormous numbers. If sentience is your test, doesn't growing your food break your own rule? And if they aren't sentient, why not eat insects?
key_points: Accept uncertainty about insect sentience and that arable farming kills many insects
Address proportionality: less cropland per unit of food generally means fewer insects affected, and harm reduction does not require perfection
Engage honestly with the fork, since uncertainty about sentience cuts both ways, instead of dodging the insect-farming half
sources: Gibbons, M., Crump, A., Barrett, M., Sarlak, S., Birch, J. & Chittka, L. (2022). Can insects feel pain? A review of the neural and behavioural evidence. Advances in Insect Physiology 63: 155-229.
New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness (2024).
Fischer, B. & Lamey, A. (2018). Field deaths in plant agriculture. Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 31: 409-428.

strongest_form: Most farm animals would never have existed without farming. If a life worth living is better than no life at all, then raising animals well and then killing them can leave the animal better off than non-existence, which is exactly what universal veganism would deliver for those animals. The vegan has to explain why preventing a good life from starting is better.
text: These animals wouldn't exist at all if we didn't eat them. If they have a decent life, isn't that better than never being born?
key_points: Address whether non-existence harms or benefits anyone in the way harming an existing animal does
Distinguish the theory (a good life) from the practice, since most farmed animals live in intensive systems with poor welfare
Engage with replaceability views and with views where each individual's life matters, instead of treating the question as obvious

Test 'they would not exist otherwise' on a case where the life is pleasant until the killing, such as happy dogs bred and kept to be eaten: if that still seems wrong, being brought into existence does not settle the question
sources: Matheny, G. & Chan, K. M. A. (2005). Human diets and animal welfare: the illogic of the larder argument. Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 18: 579-594.
Visak, T. (2013). Killing Happy Animals: Explorations in Utilitarian Ethics. Palgrave Macmillan.
Singer, P. (1979). Practical Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

strongest_form: Rights and duties come as a package: we owe obligations to those who can take part in a moral relationship and respect ours. Animals cannot enter that relationship. We may owe them kindness and a duty not to be cruel, but that is not the same as the kind of rights that would make eating them wrong.
text: Rights come with responsibilities, and animals can't take on any. Why would they have the same claim on us?
key_points: Address the contractualist argument and the fact that human infants and some people with severe cognitive disabilities also cannot reciprocate
Distinguish moral agents, who have duties, from moral patients, whose interests matter
Acknowledge that giving animals moral status does not require equal status with humans
sources: Narveson, J. (1977). Animal rights. Canadian Journal of Philosophy 7(1): 161-178.
Regan, T. (1983). The Case for Animal Rights. University of California Press.
Scruton, R. (1996). Animal Rights and Wrongs. Demos.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: A published philosophical argument holds that a diet including grazed cattle could kill fewer animals per unit of food than a crop-based diet, because ploughing and harvesting kill many field animals and one cow supplies a lot of food. The estimates are contested, but the point stands: a least-harm principle does not obviously deliver veganism, and the vegan has to win the argument on the numbers.
text: One grass-fed cow feeds a lot of people, while harvesting grain kills lots of small animals. By a least-harm standard, couldn't a bit of grazed beef be better than a vegan diet?
key_points: Address the arithmetic: critics argue the original estimates left out feed crops, per-calorie comparisons and land use
Note that field deaths are hard to quantify and that a fair comparison includes animals killed for feed and wild animals displaced by pasture
Acknowledge that least harm is shared ground and that the conclusion depends on empirical data, not on the principle alone
sources: Davis, S. L. (2003). The least harm principle may require that humans consume a diet containing large herbivores, not a vegan diet. Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 16: 387-394.
Matheny, G. (2003). Least harm: a defense of vegetarianism from Steven Davis's omnivorous proposal. Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 16: 505-511.
Fischer, B. & Lamey, A. (2018). Field deaths in plant agriculture. Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 31: 409-428.

strongest_form: People draw lines between companion, working and food animals, and those lines feel natural to anyone raised inside them. Loving a pet while eating a farmed animal need not be hypocrisy, because the relationship, not the species, may be what carries the moral weight.
text: I love my dog and would never eat it, but pigs and cows are food. Everyone treats some animals as family and others as dinner. Why is that inconsistent rather than just normal?
key_points: Ask what relevant difference separates the dog from the pig, and note that reviews of pig cognition describe complex learning, social and emotional abilities, although pigs are studied far less than dogs
Acknowledge that relationships carry moral weight, but point out that a relationship is something we create and does not decide whether the animal can suffer
Note that the line between pet and food moves between cultures and eras, which suggests custom as much as principle
Avoid accusing the person of cruelty; ask what would make eating a dog wrong and test whether that reason applies to a pig
sources: Herzog, H. (2010). Some We Love, Some We Hate, Some We Eat: Why It's So Hard to Think Straight About Animals. Harper.
Joy, M. (2009). Why We Love Dogs, Eat Pigs, and Wear Cows: An Introduction to Carnism. Conari Press.
Marino, L. & Colvin, C. M. (2015). Thinking pigs: a comparative review of cognition, emotion, and personality in Sus domesticus. International Journal of Comparative Psychology 28.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Humans have language, abstract reasoning and moral agency far beyond any other species, and many ethical traditions tie moral status to those capacities. If humans have a higher standing, weighing a person's taste or convenience above an animal's life is not obviously a mistake.
text: Humans have language, moral reasoning and culture that animals lack. That makes us a morally different kind of being, so why shouldn't our interests outweigh theirs when it comes to food?
key_points: Concede that humans differ greatly in cognitive capacity and that many thoughtful people think this matters morally
Separate 'more status' from 'no status': the question is whether a gap in intelligence justifies causing suffering for taste, not whether humans and animals are equal
Ask whether a far more intelligent species would be justified in using humans for food on the same reasoning, to test whether intelligence alone is the criterion
Note that moral concern is usually grounded in the capacity to suffer rather than in intelligence, so the burden is to explain why intelligence should count for more
sources: Singer, P. (1975). Animal Liberation. New York Review / Random House.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Most of ordinary life is organised around pleasure, and nobody demands a life-or-death justification for every choice. Eating animals is enjoyable and long established, so critics need to show it is wrong rather than assume that taste is an inadequate reason.
text: I enjoy eating meat and I'm not in danger of starving. Pleasure is a legitimate reason for most of what we do, so why does it fail as a reason for eating animals?
key_points: Distinguish necessity from preference: someone stranded with no other food is in a different position from someone choosing at a supermarket, and most vegans accept that
Ask whether pleasure alone would justify causing the same harm to a dog or a person, to test whether the person thinks pleasure is ever sufficient
Acknowledge that taste and enjoyment are real, and avoid dismissing them as trivial
Avoid claiming that nobody anywhere needs animal foods; some people live where plant food is scarce
sources: Norcross, A. (2004). Puppies, pigs, and people: eating meat and marginal cases. Philosophical Perspectives 18: 229-245. (already cited in the bank under personal-08)
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: There is no agreed method for settling moral disagreements, and moral views differ across cultures and eras. If ethics rests on conviction rather than fact, a vegan's claim that eating animals is wrong expresses a preference and has no more authority than the opposite view.
text: Ethics is a matter of culture and personal conviction, not fact. If I don't share your moral view about animals, on what basis can you say mine is the mistaken one?
key_points: Acknowledge that moral disagreement is real and that the philosophy of ethics is unsettled
Point out that subjectivism cuts both ways: it cannot show the vegan view is wrong either, and most people still condemn cruelty in other cases
Move from contested values to consistency: ask whether the person's own principles, such as avoiding needless suffering, apply to animals
Ask whether 'it's subjective' would be accepted as a reply if the victims were people, to check it is held consistently
sources: Rachels, J. The Elements of Moral Philosophy. McGraw-Hill (later editions; check the edition and year before marking reviewed).
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Once an animal has been killed, declining the meat does not bring it back, and wasting a carcass seems worse than using it. Using every part honours what was taken, and one purchase cannot change what has already happened.
text: The animal was dead before I bought it, and I cook everything, bones included, so nothing is wasted. Buying it harms nobody, so how is it wrong?
key_points: Acknowledge that the individual animal's death is in the past and cannot be reversed

Explain demand with care: retailers restock according to sales, so purchases are one input into what is produced next, although the effect of any single purchase is diffuse, which is the same puzzle as whether one person's choices make a difference
Note that using every part answers the problem of waste, not the question of whether the killing was necessary
Test the logic: the same reasoning would excuse buying any product made from harm that has already happened
sources: Kagan, S. (2011). Do I make a difference? Philosophy & Public Affairs 39(2): 105-141.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: A small holding where hens live outdoors, nothing is slaughtered and animals die of old age avoids the main harms of intensive farming. If the animals are well treated and not killed, eating their eggs, or their bodies after a natural death, is not obviously exploitation.
text: I get eggs, and meat from animals that died naturally, from a small farm or my own hens where nothing is slaughtered. Nobody suffers, so what is wrong with that?
key_points: Acknowledge that this is very different from commercial production and that avoiding slaughter removes the central objection

Raise the practical questions: what happens to male chicks, which are killed at hatching in conventional egg production, and to hens past peak laying, whether breeds selected for high egg output suffer bone weakness and keel fractures, and whether the model scales
Distinguish the small-scale case from the supermarket case, since the argument does not justify buying commercial eggs or meat
Concede that some vegans accept this case and that the remaining disagreement is about whether eating animal bodies and products is acceptable at all
sources: The influence of keel bone damage on welfare of laying hens. Frontiers in Veterinary Science 5: 6 (2018). (review; author list not confirmed)
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Well-managed grazing can build soil carbon, restore degraded grassland and use land that cannot grow crops. Comparing industrial feedlot beef with pasture-raised, rotationally grazed beef is misleading, and the headline footprint numbers average over very different systems. A vegan diet cannot replicate the ecological role that grazers play in some landscapes.
text: Grass-fed beef from well-managed pasture can store carbon in the soil and look after the land. Isn't that more sustainable than monoculture crops?
key_points: Acknowledge that grazing can sequester some soil carbon and that grassland management matters

Explain that soil sequestration is limited, saturates over time and is reversible, and generally does not offset the total emissions of grass-fed systems, which often need more land per unit of product
Include the opportunity cost of land: what the same land could store if it were restored to trees or native vegetation
sources: Garnett, T. et al. (2017). Grazed and Confused? Food Climate Research Network, University of Oxford.
Hayek, M. N., Harwatt, H., Ripple, W. J. & Mueller, N. D. (2021). The carbon opportunity cost of animal-sourced food production on land. Nature Sustainability 4: 21-24.
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.
Our World in Data. Environmental impacts of food production (ourworldindata.org/environmental-impacts-of-food).

strongest_form: Soy expansion is a major driver of deforestation in parts of South America, and vegans rely on tofu, soy milk and soya-based meat substitutes. A diet that claims environmental virtue while depending on a crop linked to forest loss is at best inconsistent.
text: Soy is wiping out the Amazon, and vegans eat loads of tofu and soy milk. Isn't that hypocritical?
key_points: Acknowledge that soy expansion is linked to deforestation in parts of South America
Present the data on where soy goes: the majority of global soy is used for animal feed, and a smaller share is direct human food
Note that cattle ranching is a larger driver of deforestation overall, and that soy can be sourced from deforestation-free supply chains
sources: Our World in Data. Soy (ourworldindata.org/soy).
Our World in Data. Drivers of deforestation (ourworldindata.org/drivers-of-deforestation).
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Food miles matter. A vegan diet built on avocados, almonds, quinoa and imported soya carries transport costs, while locally produced meat, dairy and seasonal food from nearby farms can have a smaller footprint. Telling people to cut animal foods while ignoring where their food comes from misses a large part of the picture.
text: Vegans eat avocados and quinoa shipped in from around the world. Isn't local meat better for the planet than imported vegan food?
key_points: Concede that transport is part of a food's footprint and that some foods, particularly air-freighted ones, are high-impact
Explain that transport is usually a small share of food's emissions compared with production, so what you eat usually matters more than where it comes from
Avoid claiming local food is never better, and note that local plant foods typically beat both
sources: Weber, C. L. & Matthews, H. S. (2008). Food-miles and the relative climate impacts of food choices in the United States. Environmental Science & Technology 42(10): 3508-3513.
Our World in Data. You want to reduce the carbon footprint of your food? Focus on what you eat, not whether your food is local (ourworldindata.org/food-choice-vs-eating-local).
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: A large part of the world's agricultural land is grassland or rangeland that is too steep, dry or poor to grow crops. Ruminants turn it into food, and they also eat crop residues and by-products that people cannot. A world with no animal farming would waste that capacity and push more pressure onto the cropland we do have.
text: A lot of farmland is too steep or dry to grow crops, but animals can graze it. Isn't that an efficient use of land that vegan farming can't touch?
key_points: Acknowledge that much grazing land is unsuitable for crops and that animals can use by-products people cannot eat
Address that grazing land produces little food per hectare, and that it accounts for most of agricultural land use and could in part be restored or rewilded
Engage with the case for limited rather than zero animal agriculture instead of denying that it has any role
sources: Mottet, A. et al. (2017). Livestock: on our plates or eating at our table? A new analysis of the feed/food debate. Global Food Security 14: 1-8.
van Zanten, H. H. E. et al. (2016). Global food supply: land use efficiency of livestock systems. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 21: 747-758.
Our World in Data. Land use of diets (ourworldindata.org/land-use-diets).
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.

strongest_form: Almonds are water-intensive and often grown in drought-prone regions. Replacing dairy with plant milks can swap one environmental problem for another, and treating plant-based as automatically green ignores the water and land trade-offs of specific crops.
text: Almond milk uses tons of water. Isn't swapping dairy for plant milks just trading one environmental problem for another?
key_points: Acknowledge that almonds are water-intensive and are often grown in water-stressed regions
Compare plant milks like for like (emissions, land and water per litre): on Our World in Data's figures almond milk uses less freshwater than dairy but far more than oat or soy
Note that choosing plant-based does not mean choosing almond milk
sources: Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.
Ritchie, H. (2022). Dairy vs. plant-based milk: what are the environmental impacts? Our World in Data (ourworldindata.org/environmental-impact-milks).
Ritchie, H., Rosado, P. & Roser, M. (2022). Environmental impacts of food production. Our World in Data (ourworldindata.org/environmental-impacts-of-food).
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Methane from livestock is part of a biogenic cycle and breaks down in roughly a decade, unlike CO2 from fossil fuels, which accumulates for centuries. If herd sizes are stable, they are not adding new warming. Counting cattle emissions as if they were equivalent to coal using standard 100-year conversions mischaracterises their contribution to climate change.
text: Cow methane breaks down within about a decade, unlike CO2 that lingers for centuries. If herds aren't growing, are they really causing extra warming?
key_points: Acknowledge that methane is short-lived and that GWP-star is a legitimate way to describe the effect of stable methane emissions
Explain that stable emissions still sustain the current level of warming, that cutting them would cool, and that livestock also emit nitrous oxide and drive CO2 through land use
Note that global herd sizes and totals have grown in recent decades and that regional trends differ from the global picture
sources: Lynch, J., Cain, M., Pierrehumbert, R. & Allen, M. (2020). Demonstrating GWP*: a means of reporting warming-equivalent emissions that captures the contrasting impacts of short- and long-lived climate pollutants. Environmental Research Letters 15: 044023.
FAO (2013). Tackling climate change through livestock: a global assessment of emissions and mitigation opportunities.
Clark, M. A. et al. (2020). Global food system emissions could preclude achieving the 1.5 and 2 degrees C climate change targets. Science 370(6517): 705-708.
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.

strongest_form: A relatively small number of large producers account for most industrial emissions, and fossil-fuel companies in particular have shaped the climate debate for decades. Asking individuals to change their dinner shifts attention and blame onto consumers. Policy and industry change is where the leverage is.
text: A handful of huge companies produce most emissions. Isn't telling individuals to change what they eat just shifting the blame?
key_points: Acknowledge that systemic, corporate and policy action matter a great deal
Explain that food systems are a large share of global emissions and that aggregate consumption choices shape demand and markets
Avoid claiming that personal diet change alone solves climate change
Note that the cited attribution study covers fossil fuel and cement producers whose products everyone uses, so it does not show that food emissions are a corporate problem and not a consumption one

Note that FAO estimated in 2013 that livestock supply chains alone cause about 14.5 percent of human-caused emissions, that estimates vary with method, and that much higher figures circulating online come from contested analyses
sources: Clark, M. A. et al. (2020). Global food system emissions could preclude achieving the 1.5 and 2 degrees C climate change targets. Science 370(6517): 705-708.
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.
FAO (2013). Tackling climate change through livestock: a global assessment of emissions and mitigation opportunities. Rome: Food and Agriculture Organization.
Heede, R. (2014). Tracing anthropogenic carbon dioxide and methane emissions to fossil fuel and cement producers, 1854-2010. Climatic Change 122: 229-241.

strongest_form: Sustainable farms rotate crops with livestock. Manure supplies nutrients, animals eat residues and cover crops, and grazing fits into rotations that keep soil healthy. A fully vegan agriculture would have to depend more on synthetic fertiliser or on systems that are not proven at scale.
text: Farms need animals for manure and crop rotation. Without livestock, don't we end up leaning more on synthetic fertiliser?
key_points: Acknowledge that manure and mixed rotations are real agronomic benefits and that stockless systems face nutrient-cycling challenges
Explain the alternatives (legumes, green manures, composts, recycled nutrients from human waste), and note that much manure fertilises crops grown to feed animals in the first place
Avoid claiming that vegan-organic farming is proven at global scale
sources: Billen, G. et al. (2021). Reshaping the European agro-food system and closing its nitrogen cycle: the potential of combining dietary change, agroecology, and circularity. One Earth 4(6): 839-850.

Roos, E. et al. (2017). Greedy or needy? Land use and climate impacts of food in 2050 under different livestock futures. Global Environmental Change 47: 1-12 (scenario modelling of land use and emissions, cited for the livestock-as-nutrient-recycler framing only).
Garnett, T. et al. (2017). Grazed and Confused? Food Climate Research Network, University of Oxford.
Mottet, A. et al. (2017). Livestock: on our plates or eating at our table? A new analysis of the feed/food debate. Global Food Security 14: 1-8.

strongest_form: Wild-caught fish need no farmland, fertiliser or feed, and many fish stocks are managed within sustainable limits. Sustainably caught seafood can be a low-impact protein that a purely plant-based argument overlooks.
text: Wild-caught fish need no land, feed or fertiliser, and many fish stocks are well managed. Isn't sustainably caught seafood a low-impact protein that vegans are ignoring?
key_points: Concede that some fisheries are well managed and that most fish and shellfish have lower emissions per kilogram than beef or lamb

Note that FAO assessments find more than a third of monitored marine fish stocks are fished beyond sustainable levels, although a larger share of landings comes from sustainable stocks, so 'sustainable' needs to be checked fishery by fishery
Raise bycatch, lost fishing gear and seabed damage from trawling, and that farmed fish are partly fed on crops and wild fish
Avoid the claim that the oceans will be empty by 2050, which rests on a contested projection, and keep the sentience question for the ethics items
sources: FAO (2024). The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024. Rome: Food and Agriculture Organization.
Poore, J. & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science 360(6392): 987-992.

strongest_form: Food is a personal matter. Moral views on animals differ among thoughtful people, and everyone is entitled to decide what they eat without being told they are doing something wrong. Veganism is a legitimate lifestyle choice, but it is not a universal duty that others are obliged to share.
text: What I eat is my personal choice. Why should it be anyone else's business?
key_points: Distinguish purely personal choices from actions that affect others, which can be morally evaluated
Acknowledge the value of freedom of choice and that moral criticism is not coercion
Address whether 'it's my choice' can justify an act, since choice alone does not settle whether harm is justified
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Food is how families and communities hold together: Sunday roasts, festival dishes, regional cuisines. Asking people to drop animal foods asks them to give up a piece of their heritage, and a movement that brushes that aside is not taking people seriously.
text: Meat is part of my family and cultural traditions: holidays, recipes, the lot. Why should I give that up?
key_points: Acknowledge the real value of food traditions, family and community
Note that traditions change when harms are recognised, evolve over time, and that many traditional cuisines have plant-based dishes
Avoid dismissing culture as mere habit
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Many indigenous peoples depend on hunting, fishing and herding for nutrition, cultural continuity and self-determination, often in places where farming is not viable. A universal vegan ethic can look like a colonial imposition on communities that have long, sustainable relationships with the animals they live alongside, and that makes a blanket claim of moral wrongness hard to sustain.
text: Plenty of indigenous communities rely on hunting and fishing and have done so sustainably for generations. Isn't telling them to go vegan a form of colonialism?
key_points: Acknowledge communities with few alternatives and strong cultural, nutritional and sovereignty claims, and that most vegans do not target them
Distinguish subsistence hunting and fishing from the industrial food system most people use
Engage with the worry that a universal principle gets applied unevenly, without dodging the underlying principle about unnecessary harm
sources: Kuhnlein, H. V. & Receveur, O. (1996). Dietary change and traditional food systems of indigenous peoples. Annual Review of Nutrition 16: 417-442.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Vegan diets are often presented as cheap, but meat substitutes, specialist products, supplements and fresh produce can cost more, and many people on low incomes live far from affordable shops and have little time to cook from scratch. A moral demand that only comfortable people can meet is unfair, and it risks being a position for the privileged.
text: Not everyone can afford the fancy vegan substitutes and fresh produce. Isn't veganism a privilege for people with money?
key_points: Acknowledge that processed vegan substitutes and specialist products can be expensive and that access varies by area
Note that staples such as beans, lentils, rice, oats and seasonal vegetables are typically cheap, and compare like with like
Take time, access and skills barriers seriously instead of waving them away

Cite global modelling in which healthy and sustainable diets, with vegan variants generally the cheapest, cost less than current average diets in upper-middle and high-income countries but more in low and lower-middle income ones, and note that the model left out highly processed substitutes
sources: Springmann, M., Clark, M. A., Rayner, M., Scarborough, P. & Webb, P. (2021). The global and regional costs of healthy and sustainable dietary patterns: a modelling study. The Lancet Planetary Health. DOI 10.1016/S2542-5196(21)00251-5.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Whatever the merits of veganism, many people experience vegan advocacy as self-righteous. If the aim is to reduce animal suffering, an approach that makes people defensive is counterproductive, and encouraging people to eat less meat would probably do more good than all-or-nothing demands.
text: Vegans come across as preachy and judgemental, and it puts people off. If you really wanted to help animals, wouldn't encouraging people to eat less meat work better?
key_points: Acknowledge that tone and strategy criticisms have real support, including among advocates
Separate how some advocates behave from whether the underlying argument is sound
Address the strategic question of reduction versus all-or-nothing honestly
If the person has already cut down, credit that plainly and ask what the remaining exceptions are for, to tell taste and convenience apart from a principled reason, without policing them
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Vegans use cars with rubber tyres, take medicines tested on animals, own phones built from mined materials and shop in supermarkets whose supply chains harm animals. If purity is impossible, the movement's emphasis on veganism as a clear moral line looks arbitrary, and the line could equally be drawn elsewhere.
text: Vegans still use things that harm animals, like tested medicines, tyres and phone batteries. If you can't be perfect, why is your line the right one?
key_points: Acknowledge that perfect avoidance is impossible
Explain the 'as far as is possible and practicable' framing and the difference between avoidable and unavoidable use
Avoid the all-or-nothing trap, since imperfection does not undermine the aim of reducing harm
sources: The Vegan Society. Definition of veganism (vegansociety.com).
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Some people have food allergies, digestive conditions, histories of disordered eating, or a very narrow range of foods they can tolerate. For them, cutting out food groups can be difficult or unsafe. A moral position presented as universal has to account for the people for whom it is not realistically possible, and 'ought implies can' limits how far it extends.
text: Some people have allergies, medical conditions or a history of eating disorders where cutting out food groups is risky. How can veganism be a moral duty if it isn't possible for everyone?
key_points: Acknowledge genuine medical and practical limits, and that ought implies can
Explain that the principle is usually framed as avoiding exploitation where practicable, not as demanding harm to oneself
Avoid minimising eating-disorder risks, and avoid framing exceptions as excuses used by people who do not need them
sources: Melina, V., Craig, W. & Levin, S. (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 116(12): 1970-1980.
Bardone-Cone, A. M. et al. (2012). The inter-relationships between vegetarianism and eating disorders among females. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 112(8): 1247-1252.

strongest_form: Supermarkets order in bulk and one person's purchases never visibly change how many animals are bred or killed. If my diet makes no difference to what happens to any animal, the case for an obligation to change it is much weaker, and the effort looks like symbolic gesture.
text: Even if I went vegan tomorrow, the same number of animals would be killed. My one choice makes no difference, so why bother?
key_points: Address the expected-value argument: a purchase has a small chance of tipping a supply decision, with a large effect if it does
Acknowledge that causal impotence is a genuine philosophical puzzle and that market effects are diffuse and uncertain
Note complicity and integrity arguments that do not depend on measurable causal impact
sources: Kagan, S. (2011). Do I make a difference? Philosophy & Public Affairs 39(2): 105-141.
Norcross, A. (2004). Puppies, pigs, and people: eating meat and marginal cases. Philosophical Perspectives 18: 229-245.
Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Farming and food processing support rural towns that have few other employers. A fast shift would cause real hardship, so a moral argument for abstaining has to account for the people whose living depends on the industry, not only the animals.
text: Millions of people, including farmers in rural areas, depend on animal agriculture. If everyone went vegan, wouldn't whole communities lose their livelihoods?
key_points: Acknowledge that a transition would hit rural communities hard and that this is a real cost that advocates need a plan for
Note that change would be gradual and driven by the market, with work shifting to crops, plant processing and other sectors, as in other industries that declined
Distinguish 'jobs would be lost' from 'the work is justified': employment alone is not a moral justification for a harmful practice
Avoid claiming nobody would be affected, and mention retraining and transition support as part of any serious answer
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Time and attention are limited, and many people reasonably give priority to human suffering. Treating diet as a moral priority can look misplaced while people face poverty, war and injustice.
text: There are enough human crises, from poverty to war, to fill anyone's time. Shouldn't we deal with people first before worrying about what animals eat?
key_points: Agree that human problems are serious and that people can legitimately prioritise them
Point out that it is a false trade-off: changing what you eat takes little time away from other causes, and many vegans also work on human issues
Note that if the argument worked it would dismiss every cause except the single worst one, including the person's own
Ask whether the same objection would be made to someone campaigning against dog fighting, to check it is applied consistently
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)

strongest_form: Social consensus and the law reflect long collective experience and deliberation. A view held by a large majority and written into law deserves real weight, and a small minority claiming moral insight carries a heavy burden of proof.
text: Most people think eating meat is fine, and it's perfectly legal. If almost the whole of society disagrees with you, isn't it more likely that you're the one who's wrong?
key_points: Acknowledge that consensus is some evidence about what is reasonable, and that dissenters carry a burden of argument
Point out that majorities and laws have approved practices later seen as wrong, so neither settles the question alone
Distinguish legal from right: the law sets a minimum and many legal things are still criticised
Say what would persuade you to change your own view, which keeps the exchange honest and avoids sounding certain
sources: Origin: common objection in online debate threads (paraphrased)
